stop_rule_S3_note: Counts broken reviews only: unread chunks, nonliteral quotes, wrong identity or schema. Medium confidence is a valid result that fails the ready gate.

r0010.summary: The authors state plainly that their results replicate the original study, and they only note in passing that their effect was significant in the right hemisphere rather than both. They say they cannot conclude much about that difference, so the row should stay successful rather than change to mixed.

row:1678.summary: The replication team says in its own words that it only partly replicated the original: no switching delay when results were analysed by participant, but a delay when analysed by item. Mixed fits that statement better than successful.

row:512.summary: The authors, two of whom wrote the original study, say better test scores overturn its claim that inequality grows substantially after school starts, but that part of its summer-versus-school pattern survives. They call this a partial correction, so mixed fits better than failed.

row:2447.summary: The paper says its main aim was to replicate the shift from logarithmic to linear number estimation explored by Booth and Siegler (2006), and it reports doing so for positive numbers. Siegler and Opfer (2003) appears only as background, so Booth and Siegler should replace it and the successful outcome still holds.

row:215.summary: The author's only overall statement is that he replicated Lenski's finding, because status inconsistency had significant effects after accounting for main status effects. He adds that those effects are small next to religion, but never says any part of Lenski's finding failed, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:1308.summary: The authors say their results show both similarities to and differences from Wiklund and Shepherd: two configurations confirm the original and two contradict it, while some hypotheses agree and the universal effect does not. Their doubts about generalizing the finding do not amount to an overall failure, so mixed fits better than failed.

row:1695.summary: The replicators found the same significant interaction as the original but much smaller transfer savings, and they question whether this should count as a true success. That makes mixed better than successful; failed is the closest alternative, but they stop short of saying the replication failed.

row:24.summary: The report says most of the original study's findings replicated, including the main finding, but that its results differed from the original on several parts of Hypothesis 10. That is the authors' own partly-yes, partly-no account, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:2357.summary: The authors call the study a failure to replicate in its title, in their note to the editor and in the conclusion, and they report strong evidence against the critical interaction. A supportive-context speed-up did recur, but they do not treat that as partial success, so failed fits better than mixed.

row:1523.summary: The authors repeated the hands-near-the-screen effect in the one experiment that used only the two original hand positions, but found no effect in three experiments that added more positions. They report both results together, so mixed describes the paper better than successful.

row:869.summary: If this row stays in the database, successful is the right value and mixed is wrong, because the authors call their main test an overall success and never describe it as partial. The open question is whether a study testing a model from its own protocol counts as a replication of that protocol at all, and a person needs to decide that rule.

row:2681.summary: Roodman re-ran Hjort and Poulsen's employment regressions and says his first-row results match theirs exactly or closely, so the numbers were recovered; his much weaker later results come from deliberate revisions, which the unchanged robustness code already captures. The match does not cover every outcome, as Internet usage was re-specified and the World Bank firm data were set aside.

row:1813.summary: The authors say plainly that the Kim and White (2008) effect was not replicated across all 19 schools, so failed fits better than mixed. The programme did look mildly positive in the highest-poverty schools, which the authors call consistent with the earlier studies, but that was an exploratory subgroup, and the earlier studies were run almost entirely in the kind of school where effects here were negative.

row:1345.summary: The report did test robustness: when it re-scored discernment on the original Study 2 data, the link between sharing habit and discernment shrank sharply and the authors doubted it was practically meaningful, so 'not checked' is wrong and 'robustness challenges' fits. This applies to Study 2 only, because the other studies had just a quick review.

row:629.summary: The authors did not find the step-by-step pathway they set out to replicate and favoured continuous over staged development, yet they agreed with the original on attention regulation and on how the systems integrate, so mixed is my preferred value. One opening sentence calls the findings favourable to the original model, and whether that sentence counts as an overall success verdict is a coding-rule decision.

row:2697.summary: The authors say twice that the original conclusions hold up under their alternative analyses, and the coding rules follow their judgement, so robust is supported. Some checks did weaken the result, including no effect for children under 12 months, which is why confidence is medium; the computational reproduction value stays as it is, and the combined outcome would read computationally reproducible, robust.

row:2214.summary: The original found that Polish learners often answered "How are you?" inappropriately; this replication expected the same in Russian learners, but most of their answers were rated as appropriate and the author says her hypothesis was not supported and the results differ significantly from the original. The frozen "successful" appears to confuse the learners' pragmatic success with a successful replication, though the different population, trained raters and lack of a statistical test remain caveats.

row:829.summary: The replication agreed with the original that people with more psychopathic traits and lower self-control were more willing to offend, but the original's 18% figure held only among people with no prior offending (17.5%), against 30.4% in the full sample, which the authors state in their own words. One closing sentence says the study "replicated and extended" the original; I read it as describing what was done rather than a verdict, but a reviewer who treats it as a verdict would keep "successful".

row:1796.summary: The authors say some results differ from the original study (the effect of the speaker's first language did not recur, and treatment preference went the other way) while others match it (better performance and weaker accents were still rated more favourably). That makes mixed a better fit than failed, although the abstract and any conclusion were not in the supplied text.

row:1638.summary: The replication found that people recognised pride above chance, as the original did, but not the original's gender difference, and the author sums this up as a partial replication. Mixed therefore fits better than successful, although the report is inconsistent about which gender scored higher.

row:2678.summary: The author says the original code and data gave back all the numbers in the paper, so computationally reproducible fits better than computational issues. The two coding errors he then found change some estimates when fixed, but they do not mean the published numbers could not be recovered.

row:572.summary: The authors say they replicated their main result, that blood flow in this brain region was higher in people who went back to cocaine. In the same paragraph they say they did not find the link between blood flow and hippocampal size in healthy controls that they had reported before, so 'mixed' fits better than 'successful', although the title and abstract mention only the success.

row:2018.summary: Many Labs 2 found the same effect as Bauer et al., in the same direction and clearly significant, and says the result is consistent with the hypothesis, although the effect was far smaller (d = 0.12 versus 0.87). Nothing in the paper treats part of this test as disagreeing with the original; the main doubt is that so small an effect would not reach significance in samples of ordinary size, which the authors treat as a matter of effect size.

row:2654.summary: The report re-ran the original analysis and obtained the published main result, then argued that a modelling choice about counties with repeat rallies drives it. The numbers reproduced and the conclusion did not hold up, so the computation value should change while the robustness value stays.

row:314.summary: The paper says plainly that it replicates the 2008 magpie study by Prior and colleagues, while Gallup 1970 is cited only as the inventor of the mirror test. The row's failed outcome stays correct for the new original, because the authors say their replication failed to confirm Prior's results.

row:939.summary: The authors say their designated replication closely resembled Jokela and colleagues, finding the same three symptoms linked to CRP. One link fades once extra health and lifestyle factors are added, but they treat that as an extension of the study and not as a disagreement with the original, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:208.summary: The original found that intonation added nothing beyond pauses. This replication found that it did, and the authors say outright that their results differ from the original, so failed is the right label.

row:17.summary: The authors say they replicated four of the original's five significant findings and only part of its regression results, and they reach the opposite conclusion on whether objective and subjective measures agree. Partly replicated, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:1307.summary: Two effects missed significance, including the main pointing effect at p = .06, but the authors judge from the pattern and effect sizes that they replicated the original very closely. Under the rule that the authors' overall verdict decides, this is successful.

row:172.summary: The authors say their results differed significantly from Maurer (2013): the classroom activity did not beat lecture alone, as it had in the original. Attitudes improved in every condition, but that does not preserve the original's comparison, so failed fits better than mixed.

row:1541.summary: The authors tried to repeat three blood-marker findings and say only one, lower CRP in females with substance use disorder, fully replicated, while the IL-8 and IL-10 regression results did not. The CRP-focused title does not make the whole replication a success, so mixed is the better code.

row:2658.summary: The author re-ran the original analysis, recovered its main numbers and concludes that the findings were computationally reproducible, though only from the cleaned analysis data. He also found a coding error and larger p-values on one test, but says these do not change the results qualitatively, so the change is justified with moderate rather than high confidence.

row:2682.summary: The replicators re-ran the original code and data and got every published table back, so the numbers reproduced. They also found a small mistake in the original code, but that is a separate point about the code being wrong, not about the numbers failing to come out.

row:1729.summary: The paper's appendix labels this replication unsuccessful and says nothing else about it, so the source favours failed over the database's successful. One caution: the paper's totals imply one of four such labels may be a mistake, and this could be that one, so checking the project report at osf.io/w9bza would settle it.

row:1675.summary: The replicator says in his own words that he partially replicated the original: one main effect came back and the key training effect did not. That is the database's 'mixed' rather than 'failed', even though the key confirmatory test was not significant.

row:279.summary: The original author's own lab re-ran the study twice and could not recover the original gender-dependent effects. Each study found one different significant result, but the authors attribute these to chance and conclude there is little evidence for the effect, so failed fits better than mixed.

row:2049.summary: This project re-ran 20 scarcity studies and names Chou et al. (2016) as one of only four that replicated successfully, so successful fits this row better than mixed, which describes the project as a whole. The study's own numbers are in a figure and supplement we do not have, so the evidence is the authors' label rather than a visible estimate.

row:2207.summary: The main claim that luxury goods signal a devoted partner did not replicate and slightly reversed, but the assumption that the partner paid for the goods held in both studies. Whether this row is mixed or failed depends on whether that second result counts as agreeing with the original, which only described it; I lean mixed, but this needs a rule decision.

row:285.summary: This large multi-lab study set out to repeat the 2007 hill experiment and found that infants did not prefer the Helper; the authors say plainly that it did not replicate the original, so failed fits better than mixed. They list method differences that might explain the null result, but they do not say these made the test meaningless, and the verdict applies to the hill task rather than to infant social evaluation in general.
